title: Likely Is Not Certain — Probability Models
standard: CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.7.SP.C.5 (interpret probabilities from zero to one); CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.7.SP.C.6 (compare long-run relative frequencies with predicted probabilities); CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.7.SP.C.7 (develop and evaluate probability models)
reading:
## Likely Is Not Certain

A bag holds three blue counters and one red counter. They have the same size and shape. You mix them, draw without looking, record the color, and put the counter back. Must every four draws include one red? No. A model describes chances, not a schedule.

An **outcome** is a possible result of one trial. An **event** is a set of outcomes we are interested in. Here the event is drawing red. A **trial** is one run of the chance process.

**Probability** measures how likely an event is, using a number from zero to one. Zero means impossible in the stated model. One means certain in that model. A probability of one half is an even chance. Likely does not mean guaranteed.

A **model** lists possible outcomes and assigns their chances. If each of the four counters is equally likely to be drawn, one of the four is red. The probability of red is one fourth. The probability of blue is three fourths. Colors are not equally likely just because there are two color names.

**Random** selection means using a chance process instead of deliberately choosing a result. Our bag model assumes equal chances for the individual counters. Different sizes, poor mixing, or looking into the bag could make that model unsuitable.

**Replacement** means returning the counter before the next draw. Mixing again keeps the intended setup the same. Without replacement, the bag changes. The next probability then depends on what was removed.

The **frequency** of red is how many times red occurs. Divide that count by the number of trials to get relative frequency. If red appears seven times in twenty draws, its relative frequency is 7/20, or 0.35. That does not exactly match the model's 0.25.

Small samples often vary. With many well-run trials, relative frequency tends to be closer to the model probability, but no particular result is promised. A long run of blue does not make red due on the next independent draw.

Use results to question a model. A mismatch might reflect ordinary chance, too few trials, or a poor assumption. Repeat carefully and look for patterns before deciding which explanation fits.

The next trial must repair it
short: Explain why two color names do not imply equal probabilities.
Probabilities depend on equally likely individual outcomes. Three blue counters and one red counter give different numbers of outcomes for the two colors.
What changes if a red counter is drawn and not replaced?
The stated bag then contains three blue counters and no red counters, so the next red probability is zero in that setup.
faq: No. A likely event can fail to occur on any particular trial.
Must four trials include one red?
No. One fourth is a chance for each draw under this model, not a required pattern of four results.
Does a streak make the other color due?
No. With replacement and proper mixing, earlier results do not change the next draw probability.
Does a larger sample always match better?
No. Results can fluctuate. Over many trials, relative frequencies tend toward the probabilities of a suitable model.
challenge: Our class has an opaque bag with three blue and one red counter of the same size and shape. We want to compare a model with trial results.
How closely do repeated draws with replacement match the model probability of red?
State the model. Draw without looking, return the counter, and mix each time. Record every trial. Compare separate groups of twenty draws before combining counts.
Report model probability, counts, relative frequencies, and an explanation of variation without claiming a guaranteed pattern.
facts: Probability is between zero and one.
Equal chances for counters do not imply equal chances for colors.
Returning and mixing a counter preserves the intended setup.
